Classic hangman with hotel-themed words. A quick warm-up or vocabulary recap for travel and hospitality lessons.

Project on the board and play as a whole class — students take turns calling letters. Hide the clue to make it harder, or reveal it after a few wrong guesses to give a hint. Works well as a five-minute warmer or end-of-lesson cooldown.

This is a classic hangman game with fifteen hotel and travel vocabulary words at A2 level: reception, checkout, breakfast, balcony, concierge, keycard, minibar, and more.

## Vocabulary covered

The words have been chosen to match common A2 textbook units on travel and hospitality. Each word also includes a clue to help weaker students — you can hide the clue to make the game harder.

## Lesson ideas

- **Pre-teach** the lexical set, then play hangman to reinforce
- **Review** at the end of a unit on hotels — students should already know the words
- **Vocabulary check-in** at the start of a new lesson on travel
- **Pair work**: students play in pairs on a tablet or phone, with one acting as the "host"

## Skills

Spelling, reading, alphabet recall, lexical recognition.

Eighteen meeting and project-management terms — agenda, deadline, KPI, stakeholder, pivot — with five forbidden words each. Pushes paraphrasing skills.

Split adult learners into two teams. One team-member describes the target word at the top of the card to their teammates without using any of the forbidden words. Sixty seconds per round. Correct guess = +1, accidentally using a forbidden word = −1, skip = 0. Excellent for paraphrasing practice and consolidating business vocabulary. Works particularly well with intermediate-to-advanced corporate learners.

A B2 business-English Taboo game built around vocabulary that comes up in real meetings: agenda, deadline, brainstorm, stakeholder, KPI, milestone, pivot, and twelve more.

## Why it works for adult learners

Corporate learners often "know" these words passively but struggle to explain them when they can't fall back on a translation or the obvious synonyms. Forcing paraphrase under time pressure is exactly the skill they need in real meetings — and it surfaces the gaps in their active vocabulary.

## Lesson ideas

- **Pre-meeting warm-up** in an in-house corporate course
- **Vocabulary consolidation** at the end of a business-English unit
- **Speaking fluency boost** for learners who default to one-word answers
- **Confidence builder** before a presentation skills lesson

## Variations

- **Whole-class version**: one student at the front, the rest of the class guesses
- **Written variation**: students work in pairs to write their own taboo cards using vocabulary from a recent unit
- **Harder version**: add the rule that learners can't use any French words either

Two-team quiz covering past simple, past continuous, present perfect, and a mixed category. Sixteen questions across four difficulty levels.

Split the class into two teams. Teams take turns choosing a category and a value. Read the question on the screen — the team has thirty seconds to answer. Reveal the answer to check; correct answers score the points. The teacher decides whether French or English clarifications are allowed during discussion. Great for a 30-minute review lesson before a written test.

A four-by-four Jeopardy board for B1 students reviewing the three main past tenses. Includes a "mixed" category with translation, error correction, and irregular verbs.

## Categories

- **Past simple** — affirmative, negative, and question forms
- **Past continuous** — when to use it and how to form it
- **Present perfect** — *for* vs *since*, finished vs unfinished time
- **Mixed** — irregular verbs, error correction, French → English translation

## Lesson ideas

- **End-of-unit review** before a written assessment
- **Friday treat lesson** after a heavy grammar week
- **Cover lesson** if you need an off-the-shelf 30-minute activity that any teacher can run

## How to extend

Print the question list as a worksheet for absent students. After the game, get pairs to write three new questions in the same style — a great way to consolidate.
